title: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: but the American mastodons and the existing species of elephant have tusks which do not differ appreciably, except in size, from the great spiral tusks of the mammoth, though from their comparative shortness the spiral is little developed and only appears to the eye as a gentle curve.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Teeth, beak and claw”. Scope: tusks of elephants, mastodons and mammoths (Proboscidea)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-14: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The size-only and shared-spiral predictions are direct geometric hypotheses. Existing 3D fossil and museum resources permit model comparison across all named groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit scale-normalized logarithmic spiral parameters to complete tusk centerlines of living elephants, American mastodons and mammoths, and extrapolate shorter curves with uncertainty. Shared parameters support size-only difference; significant taxon-specific curvature or torsion refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many fossil tusks are incomplete or deformed.

Sex, age and species produce substantial within-group variation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Equality of spiral parameters up to scale is a sharp comparison among three well-known tusk types. Public images and some scans exist, but complete, metrically usable tusks of mastodon, mammoth, and both living elephant species are not available as one open morphometric set. The short modern tusks are exactly the cases where a shared angle is hardest to estimate, so the test is possible on a small museum sample and not yet routine.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit one logarithmic spiral to complete tusks of mammoths, living elephants, and American mastodons, allowing only a scale difference. The claim is confirmed if a shared angle fits all three once size is removed; species differences in angle, or a scale-free shape difference in pitch or taper, would refute 'the same spiral, only shorter.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A short arc from a living elephant underdetermines the spiral angle that a long mammoth tusk displays.

Complete tusks are heavy, often broken, and less often scanned than the skulls that held them.
